edwin-nicholson-1910-08-16.A1:
Negro Shot To Death
Asheville, N. C., August 15. After declaring that he would sooner be dead than alive, Edwin Nicholson, a negro serving a six months sentence on the county roads, attempted to escape near Raleigh today and was shot to death by the guard.
edwin-nicholson-1910-08-16.A4:
NEGRO CONVICT SHOT TO DEATH
Attempts to Escape From Road Force—Investigating Cause of Wreck.
[Special to The Times-Dispatch.]
Raleigh, N. C., August 15—Edward

[Special to The Times-Dispatch.]

Raleigh, N. C., August 15.—Edward Nicholson, colored, who had served only a few days of a six months' sentence for robbing the cash drawer of W. B. Mann's grocery store here, was shot to death this afternoon while at attempting to escape from a squad of county convicts at work widening Hillsboro Street from the city limits to the A. & M. College. He ran seventy-five yards before Guard R. M. Saunders fired, the bullet taking effect in the back of his head. Strangely enough, the convict ran straight down the street toward the city, instead of taking to the woods that stretched along one side of the street. He had been heard to say that he had as soon be dead as alive now, and some believe that he really courted death by running in the open.

The investigation of the cause of the wreck in the Union Passenger Station yard here Saturday morning, that caused the death of two moonlight excursionists, and the injury of fourteen others, cannot be completed by the Corporation Commission until September 24, on account of not being able to get the members of the crews of the two trains—Seaboard and Southern—here earlier to testify. The repairs that have been in progress at the station under the train shods for the past month have very greatly demoralized the usual orderly service at the Union Station, and this has made its contribution to the cause of the accident.

The Asheville School for Girls received a charter to-day for conducting a high-grade primary school for girls in the Mountain City. The capital is $50,000 authorized and $2,500 subscribed by W. T. Weaver, S. R. McKee and others. Another charter is to the Citizen's Realty Co., Asheville, capital $25,000, by Mark W. Brown and others.

Large numbers of requests for copies of the bulletin on canning fruits and vegetables, issued by the State Department of Agriculture early in the season, are coming in to the department from other States, much to the gratification of Commissioner Graham and the Division of Horticulture in which the bulletin was prepared by Assistant Horticulturalist Shaw.
edwin-nicholson-1910-08-16.A5:
CONVICT IS SHOT
TRYING TO ESCAPE
Was Serving Six-Months Sentence—Postpone Investigation of Seaboard Wreck.
(Special to The Richmond Virginian.)
RALEIGH N. C. August 16.—Yes-

(Special to The Richmond Virginian.)
RALEIGH N. C. August 16.—Yesterday afternoon about 1 o'clock, Edwin Nicholson, colored, a convict on the Wake county roads, at work on the Hillsboro road in West Raleigh, attempted to escape and was shot and instantly killed by a guard, R. M. Sanders. The road between the city limits and the Fair grounds is being widened and a force of twenty-four convicts is at work on it. Just after finishing dinner Nicholson made a dash for liberty, heading up Hillsboro street towards the Capitol. Guard Sanders called to him to halt, but he only ran faster. The guard then asked the foreman whether to shoot or not and the foreman said "shoot," whereupon he leveled his rifle and fired, the ball entering the back of the head, causing instant death. The convict was serving a six-months' sentence for attempting to break into the cash drawer of a local grocery store, and had only been on the road force for three days.

The investigation of the wreck at Union station last Friday night, in which two lost their lives and a score of negro excursionists were more or less injured, which was started by the Corporation Commission last Saturday, has been continued until August 24 in order to allow Commissioner Rogers to take a vacation and to give time to get the necessary witnesses. So far, it seems that the wreck was due to the Seaboard engineer running his train into the station at a speed too fast to control in time to prevent the collision.
edwin-nicholson-1910-08-16.A7:
CONVICT TRIES TO ESCAPE.
On Refusing to Halt, is Shot and Killed by Guard.
Ervin Nicholson, a colored convict working with the gang on the road in the outskirts of the city, made an attempt to escape Monday noon and was shot and killed by one of the guards, R. M. Saunders. The fleeing convict was called on to halt, but refused to obey the repeated orders, as stated by those who witnessed the affair, with the result that the guard was compelled to fire, acting under orders from the supervisor in charge at the time. Saunders made a statement that is confirmed, according to reports, by the supervisor and by others who were present.

Nicholson formerly lived in Raleigh, but went away some years ago, returning within the past month and being convicted a short time since of larceny, with a resulting sentence to the roads. The coroner decided that an inquest was not necessary, since the shooting was apparently justified.

jack-nelson-cairo-1910-07-30.A1:
Lynching in Quick Order.
CAIRO, Ga., August 1.—Screams of the young daughter of John Wade, residing ten miles northeast of this place, Saturday night, resulted in the capture and lynching of a negro who had entered her room and was discovered at her bedside.

The negro, entering through a window, awakened the young girl. She screamed, and members of the family rushed into the room. The negro had no time to escape, but dived under the bed. He was dragged out from his hiding place.

News of the capture was sent from house to house among the neighbors, and a body of men quickly gathered and decided to lynch the negro immediately. He was placed in a wagon and one end of a rope was tied about his neck and the other tied to a limb. The wagon was driven from under him and his body was riddled with bullets. As there were eyewitnesses the coroner's jury did not investigate the death.

Probably Shot by Posse.

MOBILE, Ala., August 1.—At midnight last night word reached Mobile by telephone from Axis that Bill Walker, a negro, who assaulted Mrs. Nettie Gibson, had undoubtedly been shot or lynched by a posse. It reported that the wife of Jesse Brown, forced by Walker to accompany him after Walker had mortally wounded her husband, returned to Axis.

She said Walker had taken her to a water tank at Cold Creek station, near Axis, and when a train pulled up Walker tried to board it. Members of a posse were on the train and as Walker attempted to board it the posse opened fire. The woman said she suddenly realized she was free and made a dash for home. She could not say what fate Walker met.

Walker, who had been loaining around Axis, told Mrs. Gibson a friend was dead and that he had been sent to accompany her to the house where she was wanted to help prepare the body. Proceeding a few hundred feet from the Gibson home, the negro began using his knife and later accomplished his purpose. The woman was badly cut. Her eight-year-old brother, Clarence Howell, hearing her screams, ran to the scene and tried to protect his sister. Clarence Howell was also cut by the black. Walker, after forcing Mrs. Gibson to give him what money she had, left for the home of Jesse Brown, another negro. He slipped up to Brown's window and shot him while asleep. Walker then forced Brown's wife, Katie, to accompany him.

jack-nelson-cairo-1910-07-30.A6:
ANOTHER
LYNCHING
AT CAIRO
(By United Press.)

CAIRO, Ill., Aug. 1.—An investigation of the lynching of a negro caught in the bedroom of the daughter of John Wade, a white farmer living near here, is being conducted by the authorities today. The girl entered her room, and, hearing the negro, screamed. The black became frightened. He tried to escape, but the girl's cries brought help, and the negro crawled under the bed. He was dragged out and taken from the house. In a few minutes a crowd gathered and the negro was strung up to a tree.

The lynching has created considerable excitement, recalling the murder of Anna Pelly at Cairo and the lynching of Will James, the negro accused of the crime. Race feeling has been aroused.

jack-nelson-cairo-1910-07-30.A30:
NELSON IN HADES.
CAIRO, Ill., Aug. 1. — A negro named Jack Nelson was hanged last night after he had been caught in the bedroom of a Miss Wade. When the lady entered her room she saw the negro and immediately began to scream. Her cries attracted a crowd, who secured the negro and promptly hanged him.

john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A2:
Pair Taken From Scene of Crime at Luverne. SHERIFF, FEARING VIOLENCE MAKES NIGHT TRIP IN AUTO Cries of Young Woman Bring Brother to Aid. SUSPECTS WERE EMPLOYED IN HELPING FAMILY TO MOVE EVIDENTLY BELIEVED HOME WAS NOT GUARDED.
Luverne, Aug. 28.—(Special.)—Fear ing mob violence following an alleged attempted assault upon Miss Clair Fonville Saturday at midnight, Sheriff W. L. Tatum this morning rushed two negroes to the Pike County jail at Troy. The trip was made in an automobile in one hour and thirty minutes, the party having left Luverne at 16 o'clock.

Feeling among the citizens here against Cleveland Towles and John Carr, the two negroes charged with the crime, is very high, and it is said that only the prompt action of the Sheriff prevented mob violence tonight.

A few minutes after 12 o'clock Saturday night the room of Miss Clair Fonville was entered. A piece of wooden block was used to stand on to gain entrance through a window.

The man went to the bed on which Miss Fonville and her mother were sleeping and passed his hand over Miss Fonville's face. The young woman wakened and caught the man's wrists. The man then caught Miss Fonville by each arm, leaving blue places on her arms and causing abrasions on each arm.

The screams of Miss Fonville and her mother frightened the man who escaped through the window without having done any harm other than has been mentioned.

The screams brought the aged father, J. C. Fonville, and Clifton Fonville, his son, to the room. The sheriff was notified and a posse formed which soon had two negroes, suspected, charged with the crime and lodged in jail.

J. C. Fonville was preparing to move to his country home and had two negro draymen hauling his things to the depot. It is supposed that the attempted crime was planned during the day, thinking that no one was at the Fonville home but the aged parents and Miss Fonville. But Clifton Fonville came from Montgomery to spend the night with his parents and was there to save his sister.

There is said to be some evidence against the two negroes. Two tracks were discovered around the premises which fit the shoes of one negro and the shoes of the other negro had not been found Sunday morning. They made contradictory statements and both appear very nervous.

Bring Negro to Montgomery.

John D. McNeel, private secretary of the Governor, said Sunday night that he had ordered the sheriff of Pike County to bring his prisoner to Montgomery in an automobile immediately, in order that he might escape difficulty with a mob said to be forming at Luverne.

At 9 o'clock the sheriff telephoned Mr. McNeel that the automobile to bring his prisoner to Montgomery would be at the jail door within a few minutes, and that he would come to Montgomery as rapidly as possible.

Sheriff W. C. Carroll, of Pike County, reached Montgomery Monday morning at 12:15 o'clock with the prisoners. He was accompanied by J. B. Hilliard, owner of a garage in Troy, whom the sheriff swore in, for the time being, as a guard. J. B. Townsend was the chauffeur.

On the road to Montgomery the party met two cars driven by Troy people, who had been spending the day in Montgomery. At Ramer they met a car going to Luverne with several persons from that town in it. Tobe Folmar, of Luverne, identified the prisoners as Cleveland Towles and John Carr, of Luverne. Towles is a mulatto, and Carr a full blooded negro.

At the Montgomery jail the prisoners were locked up by Deputy Sheriff Harry McCord.

In speaking of the prisoners, Sheriff Carroll said they had denied the charge, but admitted having been told of the trouble, he said, by a Luverne negro. Official papers transferring the prisoners to the Montgomery County jail will be made out today. In the short time the Sheriff was allowed to get his men to Montgomery, there was little opportunity for formality.

Sheriff Carroll and the men with him left here for Troy shortly after seeing the prisoners locked up here. They said it was well they had been able to get away so quickly as they did, for he had been informed that a mob had been organized in Luverne and was headed for Troy.
john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A3:
NEGROES TAKEN
TO MONTGOMERY
TO ESCAPE MCB
Montgomery, August 28.—(Special.)—
Waking from a deep sleep in her room
at Luverne last night, Miss Claire Fon-
ville, daughter of Col. J. C. Fonville,
found the hand of a negro on her arm.

With a scream she leaped from bed
and the negro, who later proved to be
John Colvin, escaped.

After a general alarm Colvin and Cleve
Stowe, both of whom have been at work
on the Fonville place, were arrested and
at daylight rushed to Troy, 20 miles away,
for safety.

But the people were greatly stirred and
the day has been one of excitement. Early
tonight men began coming from all direc-
tions and by 8 o'clock over 300 were in
the street. Plans were made to move
early in the night, so as to reach Troy
about 2 a. m., and wreak the wrath of
the people on the accused.

The two negroes, Colvin and Stowe,
were taken from the Troy jail by Sheriff
Carroll and sent in an automobile to
Montgomery. This action was taken on
orders from John D. McNeel, private se-
cretary to the governor. The prisoners should reach Montgomery by midnight and without mishap, as the mob is more than 20 miles away. Communication was lost with Luverne after 8 o'clock tonight, the presumption being that the mob closed up the telephone office to prevent information getting out.
john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A4:
EFFORTS TO SAVE PRISONERS.
Alabama Authorities Seek to Frustrate Intentions of Mob.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., August 29. — Fearing mob violence following an alleged attempted assault upon Miss Clair Fonville at Luverne, Ala., at midnight Saturday, Sheriff W. L. Tatum of Crenshaw county yesterday rushed Cleveland Coles and John Coldin, negroes, in an automobile to the Pike county jail at Troy. Learning that a mob was being formed in Luverne to go to Troy to lynch the prisoners, John D. McNeel, private secretary to Gov. Comer, who is out of the city, ordered Sheriff W. C. Carroll of Pike county to bring the prisoners to Montgomery. The start was made in an automobile immediately. It is believed that the alleged assailants thought that the Fonville home was unprotected except by the aged parents of the girl. But Clifton Fonville, the young woman's brother, heard her screams and came to her rescue, frightening the negroes away. Feeling in Luverne is said to be very high.
john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A7:
JAILED IN STYLE.
Two Negroes Rushed to Lock-up in an Automobile.
Fearing mob violence following an alleged attempted assault on a young white girl at Luverne, Ala., at midnight Saturday, W. L. Tatum, sheriff of Crenshaw county. Sunday morning rushed Cleveland Cole and John Coldin, negroes, in an automobile to the Pike county jail at Troy.

Learning that a mob was being formed in Luverne to go to Troy to lynch the prisoners, John D. McNeel, private secretary to Gov. Comer, who is out of the city, ordered W. C. Carroll, sheriff of Pike county, to bring the prisoners to Montgomery. The start was made in an automobile immediately and the sheriff now is on the way to Montgomery.
john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A8:
NEGROES PROVE ALIBI ARE NOT INLICATED IN ATTEMPTED ASSAULT. Story of Luverne Negroes in Montgomery Jail Not Sustained in Examination, of Two They Mentioned.
Luverne, Aug. 30.—(Special)—After the published statements of Cleve Towles and John Carr, attempting to implicate two other negroes, Fate Walker and Will Earl Mitchell, the latter were put through a sweat in the city guard house and afterwards questioned closely as to their whereabouts at the time of the attempted assault on Miss Clair Fonville, while she was sleeping with her mother in a small room at the Fonville residence.

Walker and Mitchell left home about 8 o'clock and went to Brantley, a distance of twelve miles. They were seen in Brantley by reputable citizens. Walker remained in Brantley while Mitchell returned to Luverne, arriving here about 2 o'clock Sunday morning nearly two hours after the Fonville house was entered.

Cleve Towles went to the home of W. S. Sikes to help about the house at about 6:30 o'clock but when he was called to eat his supper about 8 o'clock, he could not be found.

A telephone message from the city marshal of Brantley confirms the statement of the negroes Walker and Mitchell that they were in Brantley at the time the Fonville home was entered.

It is believed generally that the right negroes have been apprehended. It is reported that the two negroes, Towles and Carr, left their home about 11 o'clock and had just returned when Towles was called for at his home and was not asleep. Carr was also in this house and went out a side door barefooted and bareheaded and went to the Hornesly home where he was found afterwards in a shed room.

It is reported that Wilks Franklin, a negro said "if the sheriff would give him a good gun, he would have guarded the negroes." This negro found himself jumping off the big railroad bridge south of Luverne. Franklin escaped but exhibits a hand which appears to have been penetrated with a pistol ball.

Progressives Want Manager. Birmingham, Aug. 30.—(Special.) The selection of a manager for the

campaign for the progressive Republican party in Alabama will take place at a meeting of the Executive Committee to be held in Birmingham Thursday of next week. It is believed that either W. F. Aldrich or Julius W. Davidson will be selected as campaign manager.
john-coldin-luverne-1910-08-28.A9:
MAY LYNCH NEGROES.
Montgomery, Ala.—A mob of 300 men left Luverne, Ala., and marched 20 miles to Troy, declaring that it would lynch John Colvin and Cleve Stowe, negroes.

Colvin was discovered in the room of Miss Claire Fonville, daughter of Col. J. C. Fonville, at Luverne. Stowe, it is alleged, was with him. They were sent to Troy to escape vengeance that seemed unavoidable.

Colvin and Stowe were taken from the Troy jail by Sheriff Carroll and sent in an automobile to Montgomery on orders from John D. McNeill, private secretary to the governor.

JUDGE GAMBLE TO PRESIDE.
Attempted Assault Case Will Be Considered at Laverne.

Luverne, Sept. 3.—(Special.)—The Crenshaw County Circuit Court will convene Monday, September 12, with Hon. A. E. Gamble as Judge. The Crenshaw court will be the first one to be held by the new judge.

It is expected that the grand jury will act promptly in the attempted criminal assault case for which two negroes, Clive Toles and John Calvin, are held.

The interested persons here, relatives of Miss Fonville, have given assurance that they want the law to take its course, but will insist that there be no delay in carrying out the law.

LUVERNE NEGROES GUILTY CONVICTED ON CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED ASSAULT. One Conducts Own Defense, But in Vain—Each Given Maximum Sentence of Twenyt Years in Penitentiary.
Luverne, Sept. 16.—(Special.)—The two negroes, Cleve Toles and John Calvin, who were charged with the attempt at criminal assault on Miss Clair Fonville at her father's home, August 27, were indicted by the Cren-shew County grand jury Tuesday and put on trial Thursday evening.

John Calvin was tried first. He had no counsel, but examined the witnesses and made a speech to the jury. He denied his guilt and set up an alibi, but failed to prove it. The trial of Calvin consumed about two hours, including the deliberation of the jury which found him guilty as charged.

The court sentenced him to the penitentiary for twenty years, which is the highest penalty.

Cleve Toles was represented by counsel and was put on trial as soon as the case of John Calvin was finished.

After the jury brought in a verdict of guilty, his counsel made a motion for a new trial which promptly was overruled by the court and Cleve also was sentenced for twenty years.

The feeling here against the negroes is at a high tension and only needs a leader to convene Judge Lynch's court. The two negroes, together with another who has been sentenced for life for killing a negro woman probably will be removed to the penitentiary this week. Miss Clair Fonville stood the ordeal through which she passed remarkably well, although she broke down and wept at one time.

A Colored Man Has Narrow Escape.
A police officer saw a colored man go into an alley between Broad and Grace on Third Street last Tuesday night. He followed him, but he had disappeared in one of the yards. He searched the yards in that neighborhood, but could not find him.

After waiting for some time he heard a gate slam and he saw the man. He called upon him to halt. He then fired at him. When he came out he saw the man standing and both of his hands raised above his head.

He was a colored man. He explained that he had been on a committee to run an excursion to West Point and the train was late getting in. He went into the lot to see his sister. The officer carried him back and found that he told the truth. The colored man lived on West Leigh Street.

It seems too that several persons were injured in a fight that took place on the excursion train to West Point.

J. E. Tignor, a white man, living in Henrico county, was arrested yesterday afternoon by Special Police man' Tiller, on the charge of disorderly conduct. Tignor was bailed for his appearance before Magistrate Puryear today.

Yesterday afternoon Tignor was driving in the county, north of Richmond, when he met an automobile in which was a number of people going from Brook Hill to Laburnum. With no apparent provocation, Tignor is alleged to have a drawn revolver and demanded that the colored chauffeur stop. Before any harm could be done, the machine was gotten beyond Tignor's range.

The chauffeur reported the matter to J. St. George Bryan, who summoned Special Officer Tiller, and went with him to where the hold-up had occurred. Tignor had not gotten very far, and when he saw the car returning, he again prepared for stopping it. He stopped his buggy and standing in the road with drawn revolver, demanded that the car stop. It was stopped, and Officer Tiller put Tignor under arrest.
